lines.text: You just fell into a hole through Earth. Where do you stop?
The tunnel is sealed and empty, and the far side is thirty-eight minutes away. On a perfect, even planet, the same fall takes forty-two. So why does the real Earth get you there four minutes sooner?
By the end, you'll see why this fall keeps perfect time with a satellite, and why a short tunnel from London to Paris would take longer than the whole planet.
First question. As you fall, does gravity get stronger, or weaker?
Only the Earth below you pulls you down. The rock above you pulls in every direction at once, so its pull cancels out.
On a perfect, even planet, that means gravity fades steadily, all the way down to zero at the centre.
But the real Earth isn't even. Its core is mostly iron, packed far tighter than the rock above it.
So as you drop through the mantle, you leave very little mass behind you, while you close in on that heavy core. Gravity actually gets stronger.
It peaks at the edge of the core, about a tenth stronger than at the surface, and only then falls to zero. That extra pull is the first clue to our missing four minutes.
So what does the ride actually feel like?
From the moment you drop, you're weightless, like an astronaut, because you and everything around you are falling together.
The pull gets gentler near the middle, but it never lets go, so you keep gaining speed, all the way to the centre.
There, gravity is zero, and on a perfect planet you're moving at about eight kilometres every second. That's fast enough to orbit the Earth.
Nothing pushes back, so you shoot straight through. Now every metre is uphill. You slow, and slow, and reach the far side just as your speed hits zero.
On the real Earth, that strong pull deep down gets you moving faster, sooner. That's where the four minutes went.
Your perfect-planet twin is still climbing, four minutes behind, toward a finish line you've already crossed.
But here's the strange part. The tunnel doesn't have to go through the middle.
Dig it at a slant, from London to Paris. Now gravity points partly into the wall, and only a slice of it pulls you along.
But the tunnel is also far shorter. And on a perfect planet, those two effects cancel exactly.
A short hop, a long one, or straight through the centre: every straight tunnel takes the same forty-two minutes.
Even a tunnel a few kilometres long, under a single city, would still take forty-two minutes.
On the real Earth, short tunnels stay near forty-two, while the longest drop toward thirty-eight. So London to Paris would take longer than falling through the whole planet.
Why? A short tunnel never leaves the outer rock, so it never feels that extra pull near the core. Only the long ones dive deep enough to use it.
So why hasn't anyone built one?
Start with air. Drag steals a little speed on every swing, so you rock back and forth, less each time, until you hang at the centre.
Then there's heat. Near the centre, the Earth is about six thousand degrees Celsius, roughly as hot as the surface of the Sun.
The outer core is liquid metal, and the pressure down there is millions of times the air pressure on your skin. No wall we know how to build would hold.

And the deepest hole ever drilled, in northern Russia, stopped about twelve kilometres down. That's not even a fifth of one percent of the way to the centre. The rock at the bottom was already as hot as an oven.
So this stays a thought experiment. But it hides one last surprise.
Remember that top speed? Fast enough to orbit.
Picture a satellite skimming just above the ground, with no air to slow it, passing overhead at the moment you jump.
On a perfect planet, one lap takes eighty-four minutes. Half a lap is forty-two.
Seen from the side, the satellite's pull toward the middle grows with its distance from the centre, just like yours does in the tunnel.
Now watch its shadow on the tunnel. It moves exactly like you. Same top speed at the centre, same arrival at the far side.
Your fall is an orbit, seen edge on. Turn the circle sideways, and the satellite simply becomes you. And every straight tunnel swings to the beat of that same orbit.
So where do you stop? In an empty tunnel, you don't. You fall, and rise, and fall again, keeping time with a satellite you'll never see.
For the thirty-second version of more ideas like this, follow What If.
